wachiman.text:
canManage() grants manage-all-groups on the VIEW scope

`canManage()` calls `hasPermission(null, VIEW, MANAGE)`, so a permission on all groups that only has the `view` scope makes it return true. `GroupsResource.java:181` calls `auth.groups().requireManage()` before creating a top-level group. An admin with view-only access to all groups can therefore create groups. The `testViewGroups` test only grants VIEW and never checks that create is still forbidden, so it would not catch this. Use only `AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE` here. The matching javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator (lines 75-76) says VIEW or MANAGE and should be corrected too.

No negative test for view-only permission

`testViewGroups` grants only VIEW but never asserts that creating a group or updating one is still forbidden. A check like that would catch the VIEW-grants-manage problem in `GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()`.

Multiple providers no longer fail fast; ties are resolved silently

The old check threw when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath. Now the provider with the highest order() wins. Default, Elytron and FIPS all return 200, so if two of them end up on the classpath the winner depends on ServiceLoader order, and the only trace is a debug log. Give the three real providers distinct orders, or keep the exception when the top two orders are equal.

Pre-built string passed as a format string

logger.debugf(builder.toString()) uses the message as a format string. Class names rarely contain '%', but use debugf("Ignored crypto providers: %s", ...) or String.join instead. The trailing ", " is also left in the message.

Dead statements in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 build ASN1Encoder objects and discard them. They have no effect, so remove them.

getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore's provider

The method returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the SUN provider and not BouncyCastle. Callers that expect BC from this method get a different provider. Consider throwing UnsupportedOperationException like the other unsupported methods, or document the behaviour.

Malformed DER gives unchecked exceptions instead of IOException

readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding. readInteger then calls read(-1) and throws NegativeArraySizeException. In readSequence a negative length is never rejected. A sequence element that reads zero bytes would make the `length > 0` loop spin forever. The signature comes from the token or server input, so reject length < 0 with an IOException, and check that each element advances.

Test uses one EC key size and does not init CryptoIntegration

KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") uses the default curve, which is P-256 on most JDKs. The ES384 and ES512 tests therefore sign with a P-256 key. Their signatures are 64 bytes but are decoded with signLength 96 and 132, so those cases only check that the round trip is stable and do not test real P-384 or P-521 signatures. Initialise the generator with secp384r1 and secp521r1 for those tests. The test also never calls AuthzClient.create or CryptoIntegration.init, so it does not cover the service-loader wiring.

Reader thread is never joined and is not a daemon

The reader thread is started and never joined. `deletedAll.set(true)` is followed at once by the assertion, so an exception thrown by an iteration still running is added to `caughtExceptions` after the assert and goes unnoticed. The thread also keeps running until it sees the flag, so a failure in the deleting loop leaves it spinning, because `deletedAll` is never set. Keep the `Thread`, set the flag in a `finally`, and `join()` it before asserting. There is also a stray whitespace-only line at 117.

Call to non-existent no-arg isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(): services module won't compile

The only definition is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (UsernamePasswordForm.java:160). A grep over services/src/main/java finds no no-arg overload, so `isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` here is a compile error.

`user != null` in the helper disables passkeys on the initial (anonymous) login page

Both call sites (lines 115 and 137) pass `context.getUser()` and are the only place `fillContextForm` runs for this form. The old code ran it only when the user was null (the anonymous page). With `&& user != null` the helper returns false for exactly that case. The anonymous page then gets no webauthn form data, and the passkey and conditional-UI login stops working there. That breaks the existing non-reauthentication tests, for example those that assert `//form[@id='webauth']` on the first login page. Re-authentication is supposed to be added to the anonymous case, not to replace it. The condition should be `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled()`. The call in UsernameForm.java:47 then needs a matching no-arg form of the check.

Missing @Override on shouldShowWebAuthnAuthenticators

This overrides the protected method added in WebAuthnAuthenticator. Add `@Override` so a signature drift is caught by the compiler.

isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is false for spawned processes, so hung flushers are never killed

The processes are created with `mp_context.Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` and `multiprocessing.Process` (`context.Process`) are sibling subclasses of `BaseProcess`. `isinstance(spawn_proc, multiprocessing.Process)` is therefore False. The old code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Now a hung ('hang' cause) process is never killed, and `_create_process_for_shards` starts a second flusher on the same shards while the first is still running. The same check at line 346 means `join` never terminates the processes. Check against `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess` or `mp_context.Process` instead, or call `kill()` unless the process is a `threading.Thread`.

join leaves later processes alive once the deadline passes

When the deadline expires, the loop `break`s before reaching the remaining processes. Those processes are neither waited on nor terminated, though `stopped` is set. Terminate the remaining processes even after the timeout. This matters more because the `terminate` branch is already skipped for spawned processes (see the isinstance finding).

time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test patches time.sleep

`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` replaces `time.sleep` globally. The added `time.sleep(0.1)` therefore does nothing, so the 'give flusher threads time' comment is false and the test can still race. Wait on a condition instead, for example poll until `messages` is non-empty with a bounded loop. Also, `test_flusher_processes_limit` never submits messages, so it only checks the shard-to-process mapping.

Inconsistent metric tag name 'shards' vs 'shard'

`wait_produce` is tagged `shards`, while the neighbouring metrics use `shard`. Both carry the same comma-joined value. Dashboards will split on the two names, so use one.

Memory info is queried once per buffer

Every `SpansBuffer.get_memory_info` calls `iter_cluster_memory_usage(self.client)`, which covers the whole cluster (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py:375). Looping over N buffers on every `submit` repeats the same query N times and sums identical values into `used` and `available`. The ratio is roughly unchanged, but the cost grows with N. Query one buffer only.

zip(error_ids, events.values()) can attach the wrong ID to an event

`nodestore.backend.get_multi` deduplicates ids and returns a dict (`src/sentry/nodestore/base.py:174-199`). It can omit missing nodes or return them in a different order than requested. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` then pairs IDs with the wrong event data once any node is missing or any ID is duplicated. The summary would show the wrong errors with no error raised. Iterate `for event_id, node_id in zip(error_ids, node_ids)` and use `events.get(node_id)`.

Error timestamps and replay event timestamps are probably in different units

Error timestamps come from nodestore event data, where `timestamp` is epoch seconds as a float (line 115). Replay recording events use the rrweb `timestamp`, which is epoch milliseconds (`as_log_message` reads `event.get("timestamp")` at `event_parser.py:182`). The merge loop at lines 153-155 compares the two directly. If the units differ, every error is emitted before the first replay event, so the chronological interleaving is wrong. The timestamp printed in the error log message would also be in seconds while the breadcrumb timestamps are in milliseconds. Normalize one side, for example multiply the error timestamp by 1000, and add a test with realistic timestamps.

Error IDs are not bounded before the nodestore fetch

`error_ids` comes straight from the replay row and is passed in full to `get_multi`. A replay with many errors causes a large nodestore read and a large Seer payload. Consider capping the number of IDs.

age/timestamp exclusivity is not enforced

The validators use truthiness of `initial_data`. `age=0` together with a `timestamp` passes, because `0` is falsy. A report with neither field also validates, even though one of the two specs requires one of them. Use `"age" in initial_data` for the exclusivity check, and add a `validate()` method that requires exactly one of the fields.

TableWidgetVisualization renders with empty columns and data

Behind `use-table-widget-visualization`, the widget gets `columns={[]}` and empty `tableData`, so it never shows the query results. This is fine only if the flag stays off. If it is enabled for anyone, dashboard table widgets render empty. Add a TODO or leave the path out until it is wired to `result.data` and `result.meta`.

get_environment_info does a nodestore fetch per issue

`get_recommended_event()` runs a query and a nodestore fetch for each issue in the comment. It sits inside a list comprehension in both the GitHub and GitLab workflows. The broad `except` hides failures, and they are logged only at info level.

Flagged table path renders an empty table, ignoring result data

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is on, `TableWidgetVisualization` gets `columns={[]}` and empty `data`/`meta`, so the widget shows no data. `result.data`, `result.meta` and `loading` are dropped, and the loading placeholder is lost on this path. I found no registration of this flag under `src`, so it can't be turned on through the normal feature system yet. If it is a placeholder, a TODO would make that clear. If the flag is ever enabled, dashboard table widgets go blank.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES is only applied while a search query is entered

The early return at line 61-63 (`if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;`) runs before the new `!HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(attribute.name)` check at line 67. With an empty search, which is the default view, `is_segment`, `project_id` and `received` are still shown. They are hidden only once the user types something. Apply the hidden filter before the early return, for example `const sorted = sortAttributes(attributes.filter(a => !HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES.includes(a.name)))`.

Possible transient 'Project not found' error while projects load

`useProjectFromId` returns undefined until `useProjects()` has the project in its list (static/app/utils/useProjectFromId.tsx:7-13). The new branch shows an error Alert whenever `replayRecord.project_id` is set and the project is not found, without checking whether projects are still loading. If the project store is not yet populated, users may briefly see a permanent-looking error instead of the spinner. Consider gating on the projects loading state.

Near-duplicate test bodies

`test_get_with_error` and `test_get_with_error_context_disabled` repeat about 60 lines of setup: store_event, store_replays, and the recording segment. Move the setup into a helper, or parametrize on the query param, so the two tests differ only in the request and the assertions.

OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes on the audit log's datetime key

The class copies `Paginator.get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor`, which expect a numeric key. The audit log endpoint orders by `-datetime`, so `getattr(item, 'datetime')` is a `datetime`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`. `build_cursor` calls this key function on the results, so every request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row gets a 500. `DateTimePaginator` (paginator.py:233-241) converts the datetime to a timestamp multiplied by 1000. A non-empty `cursor.value` would also be passed unconverted into the `datetime <= %s` filter (line 843), which is also wrong. Subclass `DateTimePaginator`, or drop the new class.

Negative-offset slicing is unsupported by Django and the comments claim otherwise

`queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`. The comment at lines 876-879 says the ORM "properly handles negative slicing" and that the path "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds". Both claims are false. The offset comes straight from the user-supplied cursor string. A client sending `optimized_pagination=true` and a negative offset gets a 500. If the slice were supported, the cursor would reach rows outside the cursor window. The 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' justification does not cover that. Remove the negative-offset branch. If efficient reverse pagination is the goal, it needs a real design, not a slice with a negative start.

Unrelated behavior change in shared BasePaginator, with a misleading comment

This edit applies to every `BasePaginator` subclass (Paginator, DateTimePaginator, and others), not just the audit log. For non-prev cursors, a negative offset is now clamped to 0 instead of failing. A tampered cursor then silently returns the first page rather than an error. For `is_prev` the offset is still used unclamped, so negative values still hit Django's assertion. The comment says negative offsets are being 'allowed', but the code does the opposite for non-prev cursors and nothing for prev cursors. Revert this hunk. If clamping is wanted, it should be a separate, tested change that also covers `is_prev`.

New query-param gated code path, with no tests and an unclear access check

The `optimized_pagination` flag switches the endpoint to a paginator that has no tests and is broken (see the findings on paginator.py). The gate `request.user.is_superuser or member.has_global_access` is not a meaningful boundary here. `OrganizationAuditPermission` already limits who reaches this endpoint, and the paginator offers no capability that needs a separate check. `is_superuser` is also not the same as an active superuser session. Remove the branch. Otherwise add tests for the optimized path and for the case where `organization_context.member` is None.

get_result is a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result

The entire `get_result` is duplicated for one extra branch, so future fixes to the base method will diverge. If this class stays, override only the slicing step. Also note that line 891 still uses the raw `offset`, which is inconsistent with the negative-offset branch.

Comment promises negative-offset support that the code does not provide

`Cursor.__init__` only does `int(offset)`, as it did before, and nothing here makes negative offsets work. The comment is misleading for readers of this core class, so remove it.

TotalDocs iterates b.cache without cacheMu while BuildIndex now writes it under a narrower lock

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock. This PR adds a call to it in `searchSupport.init` (search.go:216) and moves `cacheMu` in `BuildIndex` to cover only the map write (137-139). If any index build or event-driven index creation runs concurrently with this call, or with the metrics collector at bleve_index_metrics.go:96, the result is a concurrent map read and write, which can crash the process with a fatal error. Take `cacheMu.RLock()` in `TotalDocs`.

Init moved into the constructor; Stop's initErr no longer gates requests

`Init` now runs in `NewResourceServer`, so the constructor blocks on the full search index build and fails if it fails. That is the intent, but the `s.Init(ctx)` check was also removed from every RPC handler. `Stop` sets `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` (line 321), and that value is no longer returned to callers of Create, Update, Delete, Read and the other handlers. Requests during shutdown now go to the backend. Check that this is acceptable, or add an explicit stopping check.

Test skipped for postgres and reordering of init/watcher has no new coverage

The postgres skip in module_server_test.go is a workaround with no linked issue. The change that moves search init before the watcher and runs `Init` eagerly in the constructor is not covered by any new test.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

The class now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`. The base class leaves `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values` and the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` abstract (src/sentry/workflow_engine/processors/detector.py:142-170). `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` (src/sentry/workflow_engine/models/detector.py:86). For any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`, that call now raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class`. Before this change it returned a handler whose `evaluate` returned `[]`. `process_detectors` has no guard around the call, so one such detector aborts processing for the whole packet and for the remaining detectors. Either implement the abstract methods, or keep the handler as a plain `DetectorHandler` returning `{}` until the stateful version is built.

Stale TODO comment

The comment says "This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction", but the class is now a `StatefulDetectorHandler` subclass. The comment should be updated or removed.

Expected occurrences are built with a value that differs from the evaluated value

`test_results_on_change` and `test_dedupe` evaluate `val1` with 100 and 8, but build the expected occurrence with value 6. The mock builder ignores `value`, so the tests pass. They would not catch a bug where the wrong value is passed to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. The same applies to `test_state_results_multi_group`, where the second group has value 10 but the expected occurrence uses 6. Use the real values, and make the mock encode the value in the occurrence (for example in `evidence_data`).

Computed `config` copy is discarded; raw monitor.config is sent

`get_monitor_environment_context` builds `config` with a human-readable `schedule_type` (lines 160-162) but then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` on line 168, so the copy is dead code and the occurrence context carries the raw schedule_type. This is carried over unchanged from the old mark_failed.py, so the refactor does not introduce it. Either return `config` or drop the copy. Changing it alters the event payload, so do it separately from this move.

`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` calls `timezone.now()` when the class body runs. Every `AssignmentSource` built without an explicit `queued` (including `from_integration`) gets the process start time, not the time it was created. The field is meant to record when the assignment was queued, so the value is wrong and gets staler the longer the process runs. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)`.

Tests can't catch the stale `queued` default

`test_to_dict` only asserts that `queued` is not None, so it passes with the import-time default. Add a test that two instances created at different times get different `queued` values (for example by freezing time). Also fix the typo in the name `test_from_dict_inalid_data`.

Closing a strategy shuts down the factory-shared queue pool; after a rebalance messages are silently dropped and committed

`queue_pool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and passed to every strategy built by `create_with_partitions` (result_consumer.py:209-210, 247-259). Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy at every partition revoke, and `close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (line 338). That sets `worker.shutdown`, calls `q.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the workers, so the workers are dead after the first rebalance. The factory still holds the same pool, so the next strategy reuses it. `FixedQueuePool.submit` then calls `work_queue.put`, which raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches it (line 317), logs, and marks the offset added and completed (lines 319-325). The commit loop then commits those offsets, so every message after a rebalance is dropped and its offset committed. Fix: strategy `close()`/`terminate()` must not shut down the shared pool. Pool lifetime should belong to the factory's `shutdown()`. Alternatively, build the pool per strategy. Per-partition offset state should also be cleared on revoke.

Submit failures mark the offset complete so it gets committed without processing

When `submit` raises (decode/grouping/queue put error), the except block adds and immediately completes the offset (lines 319-325), so it is committed even though the item was never processed. Combined with the pool-shutdown problem this loses data. Even on its own, a transient error becomes silent loss, visible only in a log line. Consider letting the error propagate, or at least emitting a metric.

Docstring promises backpressure and success-only commits that the code does not provide

The docstring says 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' and 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. The queues are unbounded `queue.Queue()` (line 185), so `submit` never blocks and `poll` never pauses the consumer. Slow processing means unbounded memory growth. Offsets are also completed in the `finally` block (line 149) even when the processor raised. Either add a bound (e.g. `maxsize`, with `MessageRejected` handling) or correct the docstring.

commit function is invoked from a background thread

`commit_function` is called from `_commit_loop` on a separate thread, while arroyo normally invokes `commit` from the consumer's main thread. Is the arroyo `commit` callable thread-safe here? `close()` also does no final commit of completed offsets, so work finished after the last 1s tick is re-processed after a rebalance.

Hash-dependent assertion can flake; rebalance/reuse path untested

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts 20 random-hash groups cover all 3 queues. `hash(str)` is randomized per process, so this fails roughly 0.1% of runs. Also, no test creates a second strategy from the same factory after closing the first, which would have caught the shared-pool shutdown bug.

Error-handling test contradicts its docstring and passes only because of timing

The docstring says errors "don't block offset commits for other messages", but the test asserts that no offset is committed (line 1922). In `OrderedQueueWorker.run` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:148-149), `complete_offset` runs in `finally`, so a failed message is still marked complete. Offsets 100 and 101 therefore become committable, and the commit loop (queue_consumer.py:273-289) would commit 102. The test passes only because the loop sleeps 1s before its first commit and the test checks within about 0.3s. A slower or faster run, or a change to the commit interval, flips the result. The test should wait for the commit and assert that the partition reaches 102 despite the error. If the intent is that failures must not commit, the implementation contradicts that.

Timing-based polling is tight against the 1s commit interval

The offset-commit, gaps and error tests poll for at most 20×0.1s = 2s. The first commit only happens after the 1s wait in `_commit_loop` (queue_consumer.py:276). On a loaded CI machine this can time out and the assertion at line 1869 then fails. The loop also never fails on timeout; it falls through to later asserts. Prefer a longer deadline, or a threading.Event set from the commit callback.

Shared BasePaginator now allows negative offsets for prev cursors

The base slice previously used `offset` unchanged. Now `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`. For `is_prev` cursors a client-supplied negative offset passes straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django raises AssertionError on negative slice indexes, which gives a 500. Every paginator that inherits BasePaginator is affected, not only audit logs. The comment claims the queryset handles boundary conditions, and that is false. Cursor offsets come from the `cursor` query parameter. Revert this hunk.

OptimizedCursorPaginator passes user-controlled negative offset to queryset slice

With `enable_advanced_features`, `cursor.offset < 0` gives `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`. Django does not support negative indexing and raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so the request fails with a 500. The comment 'ORM properly handles negative slicing' is wrong. The offset is parsed from the request cursor with no validation (cursors.py:28). If the paginator ever did honor it, it would expose rows outside the normal page bounds. The paginator also duplicates BasePaginator.get_result almost entirely.

Undocumented client-toggled paginator path on audit logs, unrelated to the PR's span-buffer work

`optimized_pagination=true` switches to a paginator whose only added behavior is the negative-offset path. It is gated by `request.user.is_superuser or member.has_global_access`, a broad gate for an audit-log endpoint. This change has nothing to do with the span-buffer change in the rest of the PR. Remove the endpoint change and OptimizedCursorPaginator. Line 72 and line 89 also have trailing whitespace.

Redirect depth limit cut from 10000 to 1000

Segment trees deeper than 1000 now fail to join correctly, a tenfold reduction. The removed comment documented the tradeoff. Nothing in the PR explains the change. Spans are silently mis-grouped for deep traces.

Segments over 1000 spans are silently truncated, and the earlier size check was removed

`zpopmin` drops the oldest spans (lowest end_timestamp) once a set exceeds 1000, with no metric or log. The old behavior in buffer.py was to skip the segment with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and an error log. That check was deleted, and `self.max_segment_spans` is no longer enforced. The hardcoded 1000 ignores that setting. Data is lost silently.

Existing Redis sets are incompatible after the sadd to zadd switch

Keys already written as plain sets make `zcard`, `zunionstore` and `zscan` fail with WRONGTYPE during a rolling deploy. Also, `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` in factory.py:141 raises KeyError for spans missing the field. Consider a migration plan or `.get` with a fallback.

sum(sample_weight) silently drops events with no sample_weight

`upsampled_count` is `sum(sample_weight)`. Events stored before a project joined the allowlist, or events with no valid `client_sample_rate`, have no sample_weight. ClickHouse `sum` skips NULLs, so those events add 0 instead of 1. Charts for allowlisted projects would silently under-count with no error. event_manager.py:785-787 only sets `sample_rate` when the value is numeric and in (0,1], which confirms that some events have no weight. A fallback such as `sum(coalesce(sample_weight, 1))` would fix it, assuming the Snuba column is nullable. I did not check that.

Stale 60s eligibility cache; invalidation helper is never called

The allowlist result is cached for 60s, keyed on org and project ids. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined but nothing calls it (the option lives in `options`, and the change adds no hook). After an allowlist change, the same chart can switch between upsampled and raw counts for up to a minute. Reading an option is already cheap and in-memory, so the cache buys nothing. Remove the cache and the dead invalidation function. The comments calling it a 'performance optimization' and 'consistent behavior' do not match what the code does. The docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` also says the opposite, that it reads fresh each time.

Substring match on the query string misclassifies the discover dataset

`"event.type:error" in query` also matches `!event.type:error`, `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction`, and any query that contains that text. Those would get upsampled counts, or sum(sample_weight) over transaction rows that have no weight. It only checks the raw `query` GET param, not the parsed query. The tests cover only the plain positive and negative cases.

Alias 'count' ignores transformAliasToInputFormat

`count()` becomes `upsampled_count() as count`, so the result key is always `count`. When `transformAliasToInputFormat=1` is set, the other path presumably returns `count()` as the key. Upsampled and non-upsampled responses could then have different shapes. Please confirm this against the timeseries result code. Also, only a literal `count()` is transformed. `count()` with a different alias or other aggregates such as `epm()` stay raw, and a mixed yAxis list gets mixed semantics.

Redundant variables and misleading comments, plus trailing whitespace

`upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a pure alias. `final_columns` is recomputed in three branches even though the decision is already known at the top. Comments such as 'cached result ensures consistent behavior', 'late transformation ensures we use the most current schema assumptions' and 'better query optimization and caching' describe nothing that happens. Whitespace-only lines remain at lines 223, 234 and 278, and the formatter will flag them. The same trailing whitespace is in error_upsampling.py. Compute the columns once at the top of `_get_event_stats`.

Stray submodule gitlink committed

`sentry-repo` is a gitlink to commit a5d2909 with no related change. It looks like an accidental artifact of a nested checkout. Remove it from the PR.

Factory helper duplicates event_manager logic, with weaker validation

The helper swallows all exceptions and accepts any truthy value that converts to float. Production (event_manager.py:785-787) requires a number in (0,1]. A bad rate in a test would be stored as `sample_rate`, where production would drop it. It also runs for every `store_event`, not only for allowlisted projects. Mirror the production validation or reuse it, and avoid the bare `except Exception: pass`.

Test relies on the factory side effect and a real cache

The expected count of 10 depends on the new factory hook that sets `sample_rate`, and on Snuba deriving sample_weight from it. Only `options` is mocked, so the `cache` is real. Cached eligibility keyed on project ids could leak between tests if ids repeat. The unit tests never exercise `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, so the cache path is uncovered. Nothing tests top_events, or the discover dataset with `event.type:error`. `self.user` is also reassigned after `login_as`, which is confusing.

Denial cache key is ambiguous and ignores the folder-tree state

The denial key is built as `name + "_" + parent` (cache.go:30-32) with no separator guarantee, so name `a_b` with parent `c` and name `a` with parent `b_c` give the same key. Kubernetes names rarely contain `_`, but the key can still collide. Also, a denial is stored for shortCacheTTL (30s, line 32). A grant made during that window is ignored, because the denial check runs before the permission cache and the DB. Before this change a denial was never cached on its own. Check that this staleness is acceptable. Consider a separator that cannot occur in names, such as a NUL byte or a length prefix.

Cache-miss metric also counts identity lookup errors and cached-but-denied results

`permissionCacheUsage("false")` is incremented whenever the cached path does not return Allowed. That includes a cache hit where the permission was not in the cached map, a render-service request (always uncached), and a GetUserIdentifiers error. The metric therefore mixes real misses with these cases. Previously it only counted a miss on permCache.Get.
